setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient on volume-control ventilation suddenly has peak airway pressure rise from 28 to 45 cmH2O, while plateau pressure remains 20 cmH2O. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Bronchospasm or endotracheal tube obstruction by secretions
options.D: Right main bronchus intubation causing collapse of the left lung

explanation: Peak pressure reflects both resistive and elastic loads; plateau pressure (measured during an inspiratory pause with no flow) reflects elastic recoil of the respiratory system. A rise in peak pressure with unchanged plateau indicates increased airway resistance (bronchospasm, secretions, kinked or bitten tube). The other options reduce compliance and raise plateau pressure.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: In a patient on volume control, both peak and plateau pressures rise by 15 cmH2O over 30 minutes. Which cause is most likely?

options.A: Reduced respiratory system compliance, e.g. pneumothorax or worsening oedema
options.C: Partial obstruction of the endotracheal tube by thick secretions or a kinked tube

explanation: When peak and plateau pressures rise together with an unchanged gradient, the problem is decreased compliance of the lung, pleura or chest wall (pneumothorax, atelectasis, endobronchial intubation, pulmonary oedema, abdominal distension). Resistive problems widen the peak–plateau gap.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A passive patient on volume control has tidal volume 500 mL, plateau pressure 25 cmH2O and PEEP 5 cmH2O. What is the static respiratory system compliance?
explanation: Static compliance = tidal volume / (plateau pressure − total PEEP) = 500 / (25 − 5) = 25 mL/cmH2O. Normal values in ventilated patients are about 50–100 mL/cmH2O; low values are typical of ARDS. If intrinsic PEEP is present, total PEEP should be used.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: During constant-flow volume control at 60 L/min, peak pressure is 40 cmH2O and plateau pressure 20 cmH2O. What is the inspiratory airway resistance?
explanation: Resistance = (peak − plateau pressure) / flow. A flow of 60 L/min is 1 L/s, so resistance = (40 − 20) / 1 = 20 cmH2O/L/s. Normal intubated values are about 5–15 cmH2O/L/s, including tube resistance.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: How is intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP) measured in a passive, ventilated patient?

options.B: Performing an end-inspiratory hold and reading the plateau pressure above PEEP
options.D: Measuring peak airway pressure during a cough
options.E: An end-expiratory occlusion hold, reading airway pressure above set PEEP

explanation: An end-expiratory hold occludes the circuit at the end of expiration, allowing alveolar and circuit pressures to equilibrate; the measured pressure minus set PEEP equals intrinsic PEEP. The test requires a relaxed patient without active expiration or breathing efforts.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; GOLD 2025 report [79]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: On the flow–time waveform of a ventilated patient with COPD, expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath. What does this indicate?

options.B: Excessive inspiratory time with normal expiration

explanation: If expiratory flow is still present when the next breath starts, lung emptying is incomplete, causing gas trapping and intrinsic PEEP. Management includes reducing minute ventilation, lowering respiratory rate, shortening inspiratory time, and treating bronchospasm.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: In pressure-controlled ventilation, what happens to tidal volume if respiratory system compliance falls because of worsening pulmonary oedema, with all settings unchanged?

options.D: Peak pressure rises above the set inspiratory pressure
options.E: Tidal volume remains constant and peak pressure rises

explanation: In pressure control, the ventilator delivers a set inspiratory pressure; tidal volume depends on compliance, resistance and inspiratory time. Lower compliance means a smaller tidal volume for the same driving pressure, risking hypoventilation. In volume control, pressure would rise instead.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which statement correctly describes pressure-regulated volume control (PRVC) or similar adaptive modes?

options.B: It is a spontaneous mode with no mandatory breaths
options.C: Tidal volume is variable and pressure is fixed, regardless of the set volume target
options.D: Flow is constant and pressure is uncontrolled
options.E: Inspiratory pressure is adjusted breath by breath to deliver a target tidal volume

explanation: PRVC is a dual-control mode delivering pressure-controlled breaths with automatic adjustment of the inspiratory pressure to reach a target tidal volume. A drawback is that strong patient effort can reduce the delivered pressure, reducing support when demand is highest.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient with severe COPD on pressure support shows active expiratory effort at the end of inspiration and a prolonged inspiratory time. Which adjustment is most appropriate?

options.A: Decrease the expiratory trigger to 5% of peak flow to prolong inspiratory time
options.C: Switch the inspiratory trigger from flow to pressure
options.D: Increase the expiratory trigger (cycle-off) percentage, e.g. from 25% to 45%
options.E: Increase the pressure support level by 10 cmH2O

explanation: Pressure support breaths cycle to expiration when inspiratory flow falls to a set percentage of peak flow. In COPD, high resistance and long time constants slow the flow decay, causing delayed cycling. Increasing the cycle-off threshold shortens inspiration, improving synchrony and reducing hyperinflation.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient with COPD on pressure support has visible inspiratory efforts that fail to trigger the ventilator. Intrinsic PEEP is 10 cmH2O and set PEEP is 3 cmH2O. Which change best reduces ineffective triggering?

options.B: Increase external PEEP to about 7–8 cmH2O

explanation: With intrinsic PEEP, the patient must generate enough effort to overcome it before the ventilator senses a trigger. Applying external PEEP at about 75–85% of intrinsic PEEP reduces the triggering threshold without worsening hyperinflation. Excessive pressure support can worsen hyperinflation and missed triggers.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; GOLD 2025 report [79]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A dyspnoeic patient on volume control with a set flow of 35 L/min has a pressure–time waveform showing a concave "scooped-out" inspiratory limb. What is the best adjustment?

options.B: Decrease the inspiratory flow rate to improve the distribution of gas
options.C: Increase inspiratory flow or switch to a pressure-targeted mode
options.E: Increase the inspiratory pause time to improve oxygenation

explanation: A concave inspiratory pressure limb in volume control indicates that the patient's inspiratory demand exceeds the delivered flow (flow starvation), increasing work of breathing. Increasing flow or using pressure-targeted modes, where flow varies with demand, improves synchrony.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A sedated patient on pressure support has a respiratory rate of 34/min with no visible respiratory effort. A cuff leak is noted. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Auto-triggering from the leak lowering circuit pressure or flow
options.C: Severe metabolic acidosis driving a high spontaneous respiratory rate

explanation: Auto-triggering occurs when the ventilator senses a pressure or flow change not generated by the patient, such as circuit or cuff leaks, water in the tubing or cardiac oscillations with very sensitive triggers. It causes respiratory alkalosis and hyperinflation; fixing the leak or adjusting trigger sensitivity resolves it.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A deeply sedated patient on controlled ventilation shows a diaphragmatic contraction that starts after each machine-initiated breath, sometimes causing a second breath. What is this phenomenon called?

options.B: Premature cycling caused by low flow

explanation: Reverse triggering is a respiratory entrainment in which a passive insufflation triggers diaphragmatic contraction, often in deeply sedated patients. It may cause breath stacking (double triggering) with large tidal volumes and potentially injurious pendelluft. Adjusting sedation or ventilator rate can help.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A man is 170 cm tall and weighs 110 kg. What tidal volume corresponds to 6 mL/kg predicted body weight?
explanation: Predicted body weight for men = 50 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) = 50 + 0.91 × 17.6 ≈ 66 kg. Tidal volume at 6 mL/kg = 396 mL, about 400 mL. Actual body weight must not be used because lung size relates to height and sex.
referenceText: ARDS Network 2000 (ARMA low tidal volume) [207]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A woman is 160 cm tall. What is her predicted body weight according to the ARDSNet formula?
explanation: For women, PBW = 45.5 + 0.91 × (height in cm − 152.4) = 45.5 + 0.91 × 7.6 ≈ 52.4 kg. A tidal volume of 6 mL/kg PBW would therefore be about 315 mL. The female formula is 4.5 kg lower than the male formula for the same height.
referenceText: ARDS Network 2000 (ARMA low tidal volume) [207]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A ventilated patient has PaCO2 60 mmHg at a respiratory rate of 15/min with fixed tidal volume. Assuming constant CO2 production and dead space fraction, which respiratory rate is needed to reach PaCO2 45 mmHg?
explanation: PaCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation. New rate = current rate × current PaCO2 / target PaCO2 = 15 × 60 / 45 = 20/min. In practice, increasing rate may shorten expiratory time and increase dead space, so reassessment is required.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient has PaCO2 50 mmHg and mixed expired PCO2 of 20 mmHg. What is the physiological dead space fraction (VD/VT)?
explanation: The Bohr–Enghoff equation gives VD/VT = (PaCO2 − PECO2) / PaCO2 = (50 − 20) / 50 = 0.6. Normal VD/VT is about 0.3; high values in ARDS are associated with increased mortality.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient breathing room air at sea level has PaO2 55 mmHg and PaCO2 40 mmHg. Using a respiratory quotient of 0.8, what is the approximate alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient?
explanation: PAO2 = FiO2 × (760 − 47) − PaCO2 / 0.8 = 0.21 × 713 − 50 ≈ 150 − 50 = 100 mmHg. A–a gradient = 100 − 55 = 45 mmHg, which is elevated (normal about 5–20 mmHg, increasing with age), indicating a gas-exchange abnormality rather than pure hypoventilation.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient with lobar pneumonia has PaO2 58 mmHg on FiO2 0.4 and only rises to 62 mmHg on FiO2 1.0. Which mechanism best explains the hypoxaemia?
explanation: Shunt (perfusion of unventilated alveoli) causes hypoxaemia that responds poorly to supplemental oxygen, because shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas. V/Q mismatch, diffusion limitation and hypoventilation respond well to increased FiO2. Shunt improves with recruitment and PEEP.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A ventilated patient has mean airway pressure 20 cmH2O, FiO2 0.8 and PaO2 80 mmHg. What is the oxygenation index?
explanation: Oxygenation index = (FiO2 × 100 × mean airway pressure) / PaO2 = (80 × 20) / 80 = 20. Unlike the P/F ratio, it incorporates the intensity of ventilatory support; values above about 25–40 indicate severe hypoxaemic failure and may prompt consideration of ECMO.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which mechanism of ventilator-induced lung injury results from repetitive opening and closing of unstable alveoli at low end-expiratory volumes?
explanation: Atelectrauma is caused by cyclic recruitment–derecruitment, generating shear stress at the interfaces of open and collapsed lung; adequate PEEP reduces it. Volutrauma results from overdistension; barotrauma refers to air leaks; biotrauma is the release of inflammatory mediators from injured lung.
referenceText: ARDS Network 2000 (ARMA low tidal volume) [207]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which set of ventilator variables contributes to "mechanical power", the energy delivered to the respiratory system per minute?

options.B: Tidal volume, rate, driving pressure, PEEP and inspiratory flow
options.D: Cuff pressure, endotracheal tube size and humidifier temperature

explanation: Mechanical power combines tidal volume, driving pressure, respiratory rate, flow and PEEP into a single estimate of the energy transferred to the lung per minute (J/min). Higher mechanical power is associated with lung injury and mortality, emphasising that rate as well as volume and pressure matters.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Amato et al. 2015 (driving pressure) [3]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A morbidly obese patient with ARDS has plateau pressure 34 cmH2O. Why may an oesophageal balloon help set PEEP?

options.B: It measures cardiac output via oesophageal Doppler to guide PEEP and fluid therapy decisions
options.C: Pleural pressure is often high, so transpulmonary pressure is lower than plateau suggests
options.D: It replaces the need to measure plateau pressure
options.E: It directly measures alveolar oxygen tension

explanation: Transpulmonary pressure equals airway pressure minus pleural (oesophageal) pressure. In obesity or abdominal hypertension, high pleural pressure makes plateau pressure overestimate lung stress and may cause collapse at low PEEP; oesophageal manometry enables PEEP titration to keep end-expiratory transpulmonary pressure slightly positive.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Grasselli et al. 2023 (ESICM ARDS guideline) [81]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What is the principal haemodynamic effect of applying high PEEP in a hypovolaemic patient?

options.A: Reduced venous return and cardiac output
options.B: Reduced right ventricular afterload in all patients
options.E: Increased venous return and cardiac output

explanation: Positive intrathoracic pressure reduces the venous return gradient, decreasing right ventricular preload, especially in hypovolaemia. High PEEP can also increase pulmonary vascular resistance and RV afterload. By contrast, positive pressure reduces LV afterload, which may benefit patients with LV failure.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient is ventilated with FiO2 1.0 for many hours. Which complication results from nitrogen washout of poorly ventilated alveoli?

options.A: Hypercapnic respiratory acidosis from loss of hypoxic drive in all patients

explanation: High FiO2 replaces nitrogen in alveoli; in low V/Q units the oxygen is absorbed faster than it is replaced, causing absorption atelectasis and increased shunt. Hyperoxia also produces oxidative injury. FiO2 should be titrated to the lowest level achieving target saturations.
referenceText: Siemieniuk et al. 2018 (oxygen therapy guideline) [197]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: In airway pressure release ventilation (APRV), how is the release time (T-low) usually set?

options.A: Long enough for expiratory flow to reach zero, ensuring complete lung emptying each cycle
options.C: Short enough to end expiration when flow falls to about 50–75% of peak expiratory flow
options.D: Adjusted to achieve a PaCO2 of 25 mmHg
options.E: Set at 3 seconds in all patients

explanation: APRV maintains a prolonged high pressure (P-high) with brief releases to a low pressure (P-low, often zero). T-low is set to terminate the release before full exhalation (commonly at 50–75% of peak expiratory flow), generating intrinsic PEEP to prevent derecruitment while allowing spontaneous breathing.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What was the main finding of the OSCILLATE trial of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) in early moderate-to-severe ARDS?

options.A: HFOV improved survival only in severe hypercapnia
options.C: HFOV increased in-hospital mortality versus low tidal volume, high PEEP
options.D: HFOV reduced the need for sedation
options.E: HFOV reduced ICU length of stay and sedation needs without any effect on mortality

explanation: OSCILLATE was stopped early because of higher in-hospital mortality with HFOV (47% vs 35%), associated with more sedation, neuromuscular blockade and vasoactive use. OSCAR showed no benefit. Guidelines recommend against routine HFOV in ARDS.
referenceText: Ferguson et al. 2013 (OSCILLATE) [68]; Grasselli et al. 2023 (ESICM ARDS guideline) [81]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A ventilated patient suddenly desaturates to 78% and the capnography waveform disappears. What is the most likely cause and immediate action?

options.A: Tube displacement or obstruction; hand-ventilate with 100% oxygen and check the tube
options.C: Bronchospasm; give nebulised salbutamol and continue the current ventilation unchanged
options.D: Ventilator failure; replace the ventilator before assessing the patient

explanation: Loss of capnography with acute desaturation suggests extubation, oesophageal displacement or complete tube obstruction. The DOPE mnemonic (displacement, obstruction, pneumothorax, equipment) guides assessment; disconnecting and hand-bagging with 100% oxygen separates patient from equipment problems.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What is the recommended range for endotracheal tube cuff pressure?

options.D: Inflate until no leak, regardless of pressure

explanation: Cuff pressure should be maintained at 20–30 cmH2O. Pressures below 20 cmH2O allow microaspiration of subglottic secretions (VAP risk), whereas pressures above 30 cmH2O impair tracheal mucosal perfusion, risking ischaemia, stenosis and tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
referenceText: Klompas et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC VAP prevention) [115]; Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A heat and moisture exchanger (HME) is used in a ventilated patient with ARDS and severe hypercapnia. What disadvantage is most relevant?

options.C: It adds dead space and resistance, worsening CO2 clearance
options.D: It reduces tidal volume delivery by 50%
options.E: It eliminates the need for humidification and so dries secretions

explanation: HMEs add dead space (typically 50–100 mL) and resistance, which matter when small tidal volumes are used. Heated humidifiers are preferred in ARDS with hypercapnia, copious or bloody secretions, and large leaks.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: According to Poiseuille's law, what happens to resistance to laminar flow if the radius of an airway or tube is halved?
explanation: Poiseuille's law states that resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (R = 8ηl / πr⁴). Halving the radius increases resistance by 2⁴ = 16 times. Small endotracheal tubes and secretions therefore greatly increase work of breathing.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which condition is necessary for an accurate plateau pressure measurement?

options.A: A passive patient with an end-inspiratory pause of 0.5–1 second
options.C: High inspiratory flow during the measurement
options.E: An actively breathing patient on pressure support with a short pause

explanation: Plateau pressure is measured during an end-inspiratory occlusion when flow is zero, so it reflects elastic recoil. Patient inspiratory effort lowers and expiratory effort raises the measured value, making it unreliable. In pressure support, an inspiratory hold can be attempted but interpretation is difficult.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; ARDS Network 2000 (ARMA low tidal volume) [207]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: On constant-flow volume control, the pressure–time curve during inspiration shows upward concavity (progressive steepening). What does this suggest?

options.B: Patient inspiratory effort causing flow starvation

explanation: The stress index describes the shape of the pressure–time curve during constant flow. Upward concavity (stress index above 1) suggests overdistension, so PEEP or tidal volume should be reduced; downward concavity (below 1) suggests tidal recruitment; a straight line suggests linear compliance.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: To increase expiratory time in a ventilated patient with severe bronchospasm, which change is most effective?
explanation: Expiratory time is the cycle time minus inspiratory time. Reducing respiratory rate produces the largest increase in expiratory time; increasing inspiratory flow and removing inspiratory pause shorten inspiration. Decreasing flow, adding a pause and increasing rate all shorten expiratory time and worsen air trapping.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; GINA 2024 report [78]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What signal does neurally adjusted ventilatory assist (NAVA) use to trigger, size and cycle breaths?

options.D: Inspiratory flow measured at the Y-piece by a proximal flow sensor near the patient
options.E: Diaphragmatic electrical activity recorded by an oesophageal catheter

explanation: NAVA uses diaphragmatic electrical activity (Edi) recorded by electrodes on a nasogastric catheter. Support is proportional to Edi, and triggering is independent of intrinsic PEEP and leaks, improving patient–ventilator synchrony.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which bedside measurement on the ventilator is used to estimate respiratory drive in spontaneously breathing patients?

options.A: Peak inspiratory pressure during assisted breaths

explanation: P0.1 is the drop in airway pressure during the first 100 ms of an occluded inspiration, which reflects neural drive and is independent of muscle weakness and patient effort perception. Values above about 3.5–4 cmH2O suggest high drive and risk of self-inflicted lung injury.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Grasselli et al. 2023 (ESICM ARDS guideline) [81]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: During lung-protective ventilation for ARDS, the PaCO2 rises to 65 mmHg with pH 7.24. The patient has no raised intracranial pressure. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.B: Give sodium bicarbonate to normalise the pH to 7.40 within the next hour
options.C: Increase tidal volume to 10 mL/kg PBW
options.E: Accept permissive hypercapnia, as pH remains above about 7.15–7.20

explanation: Permissive hypercapnia is accepted to limit tidal volumes and pressures; the ARMA protocol allowed pH down to 7.15 with rate increases up to 35/min before considering bicarbonate. Hypercapnia is contraindicated in raised intracranial pressure and may worsen RV failure.
referenceText: ARDS Network 2000 (ARMA low tidal volume) [207]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A ventilated patient has severe right lower lobe pneumonia with hypoxaemia. Which positioning is most likely to improve oxygenation?

options.A: Lateral position with the affected (right) lung dependent
options.D: Lateral position with the good (left) lung dependent

explanation: Gravity increases perfusion to the dependent lung; placing the good lung down improves V/Q matching and oxygenation in unilateral disease. Exceptions include massive haemoptysis or lung abscess, where the affected lung is placed down to protect the healthy lung from spillage.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A ventilated patient has a large bronchopleural fistula with a big air leak through the chest drain. Which ventilation strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Apply high suction to the chest drain to maximise leak flow
options.B: Minimise airway pressures, tidal volume, PEEP and inspiratory time
options.C: Increase PEEP to 18 cmH2O to splint the fistula and recruit lung
options.E: High tidal volumes to compensate for the volume lost through the leak

explanation: Fistula flow depends on transpulmonary pressure and inspiratory duration. Strategies include low tidal volume, low PEEP, short inspiratory time, reduced respiratory rate, permissive hypercapnia and minimal chest drain suction; independent lung ventilation or endobronchial valves are options for refractory cases.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Roberts et al. 2023 (BTS pleural disease) [180]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which capnography waveform pattern is characteristic of bronchospasm?

options.B: A square waveform with a flat plateau
options.D: A sloping phase II and III with a "shark-fin" appearance
options.E: Cardiogenic oscillations during the expiratory pause

explanation: Bronchospasm causes uneven emptying of lung units with varying time constants, producing a prolonged upslope and loss of the alveolar plateau (shark fin). A sudden drop to zero suggests disconnection or extubation; a raised baseline indicates rebreathing.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: In a ventilated patient with a large increase in alveolar dead space, how does end-tidal CO2 relate to PaCO2?

options.C: The PaCO2–ETCO2 gap widens, so ETCO2 underestimates PaCO2
options.D: Dead space has no effect on the PaCO2–ETCO2 gradient

explanation: Normally ETCO2 is 2–5 mmHg below PaCO2. Increased alveolar dead space (pulmonary embolism, low cardiac output, hyperinflation) dilutes expired CO2 with gas from unperfused alveoli, widening the gap. ETCO2 trends must therefore be calibrated against arterial gases.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What did the HOT-ICU trial show when comparing a PaO2 target of 60 mmHg with 90 mmHg in ICU patients with acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure?

options.B: More ischaemic events in the 90 mmHg group
options.C: More delirium in the 60 mmHg group
options.D: Lower mortality in the 60 mmHg group
options.E: Lower mortality in the 90 mmHg group

explanation: HOT-ICU randomised 2928 patients and found no difference in 90-day mortality or serious adverse events between lower (PaO2 60 mmHg) and higher (90 mmHg) targets. Guidelines advise avoiding both hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia, commonly targeting SpO2 around 92–96% in most patients.
referenceText: Schjørring et al. 2021 (HOT-ICU) [190]; Siemieniuk et al. 2018 (oxygen therapy guideline) [197]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: On a static pressure–volume curve of an ARDS lung, what does the lower inflection point represent?

options.C: The pressure at which substantial alveolar recruitment begins
options.D: The point at which maximal alveolar overdistension begins

explanation: The lower inflection point marks a sudden increase in compliance as collapsed alveoli start to open. Setting PEEP slightly above it was previously proposed to prevent derecruitment. The upper inflection point indicates the onset of overdistension; recruitment actually continues along the curve.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: In volume-controlled ventilation, how does a decelerating (ramp) flow pattern compare with a square-wave flow at the same tidal volume and inspiratory time?

options.C: It produces a lower peak airway pressure and a higher mean airway pressure
options.D: It produces a higher peak airway pressure and lower mean airway pressure

explanation: A decelerating flow delivers most of the volume early in inspiration, lowering the peak pressure and increasing mean airway pressure, which may improve gas distribution and oxygenation. Square-wave flow allows simple calculation of resistance.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Which statement about ventilator triggering is correct?

options.A: Triggering sensitivity has no effect on the patient's work of breathing or on asynchrony rates
options.B: Pressure triggering is unaffected by intrinsic PEEP
options.D: Time triggering depends on patient effort
options.E: Flow triggering usually needs less effort, with a shorter delay, than pressure triggering

explanation: Flow triggering detects a drop in the continuous bias flow returning to the ventilator and responds faster than pressure triggering. Both are affected by intrinsic PEEP. Overly sensitive triggers can cause auto-triggering from leaks or cardiac oscillations.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: After emergency intubation, a patient has reduced breath sounds on the left, SpO2 88% and a tube depth of 27 cm at the lips. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: In adults, the tube tip should lie 2–6 cm above the carina, typically at 21–23 cm at the lips. A deep tube usually enters the right main bronchus because of its more vertical angle, causing left lung collapse and hypoxaemia. Withdrawing the tube after deflating the cuff corrects the problem.
referenceText: Higgs et al. 2018 (DAS/ICS critically ill intubation) [91]; Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What is a major risk of inverse-ratio ventilation (inspiratory time longer than expiratory time)?

options.A: Reduction in mean airway pressure and resulting hypoxaemia
options.E: Gas trapping and haemodynamic compromise from intrinsic PEEP

explanation: Prolonging inspiration increases mean airway pressure and can improve oxygenation, but the shorter expiratory time risks incomplete emptying, intrinsic PEEP, barotrauma and hypotension. It also usually requires deep sedation.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: A patient with opioid overdose breathing room air has PaO2 55 mmHg and PaCO2 76 mmHg. What does the alveolar–arterial gradient suggest?

options.A: Diffusion limitation is the main mechanism
options.B: A normal A–a gradient, indicating pure hypoventilation
options.C: A negative A–a gradient, indicating laboratory error
options.D: A–a gradient cannot be calculated on room air
options.E: A markedly increased A–a gradient, indicating shunt

explanation: PAO2 = 150 − 76 / 0.8 = 150 − 95 = 55 mmHg; with PaO2 55, the A–a gradient is about 0 (within normal limits), consistent with pure alveolar hypoventilation. Treating the cause (e.g. naloxone) corrects both hypoxaemia and hypercapnia.
referenceText: Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: What is the time constant of the respiratory system and its relevance?

options.A: The ratio of PEEP to plateau pressure
options.B: Resistance × compliance, which determines how quickly the lung fills and empties
options.C: The ratio of tidal volume to respiratory rate, which sets the inspiratory time and flow
options.D: The product of FiO2 and mean airway pressure
options.E: The time to reach peak inspiratory flow

explanation: The time constant (τ = R × C) determines the speed of passive emptying; about 3 time constants are needed for 95% exhalation. Diseases with high resistance (COPD, asthma) have long time constants and need longer expiratory times to avoid gas trapping.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]

setTitle: Mechanical Ventilation: Principles, Modes and Monitoring
stem: Immediately after intubation, a patient with severe asthma becomes profoundly hypotensive with rising airway pressures. What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.A: Start an adrenaline infusion and fluid bolus immediately, without changing any ventilator settings
options.B: Disconnect from the ventilator for 30–60 seconds to allow exhalation, and assess for pneumothorax
options.C: Increase the respiratory rate to correct the acidosis
options.E: Give 2 L of fluid and continue ventilation unchanged

explanation: Dynamic hyperinflation from excessive ventilation is a common cause of post-intubation hypotension in asthma. A brief disconnection allows trapped gas to escape, and improvement confirms the diagnosis. Afterwards, low rate, small tidal volume and long expiratory time are used; tension pneumothorax must be excluded.
referenceText: Tobin 2013 (Principles and Practice of Mechanical Ventilation) [213]; GINA 2024 report [78]
